topics.name: Basics
topics.description: Foundations of algorithmic thinking. Big-O analysis, primitive math operations, modular arithmetic, overflow safety, simulation, and the iterative control-flow patterns every later topic depends on. If you cannot reason precisely about an `O(N)` loop here, no later topic will work for you.
learning_outcomes: Compute time and space complexity from first principles, including amortized analysis
Translate prose problem statements into clean iterative simulations
Apply integer math, modular arithmetic, GCD/LCM, prime sieve, and overflow-safe operations
Identify when a naive simulation is provably correct and when it must be optimized

topics.name: Sorting
topics.description: Comparison and non-comparison sorting algorithms, their invariants, and when each one is the right tool. Sorting is rarely the question itself — it's the preprocessing step that unlocks two-pointer, greedy, binary-search, and interval techniques across the rest of the curriculum.
learning_outcomes: Implement merge sort, quicksort, heapsort, and counting sort from scratch
Pick the right sort given constraints (stability, in-place, integer-bounded keys)
Use custom comparators to encode multi-key ordering and tie-breaking
Solve k-th-element problems via partial sorts and quickselect

topics.name: Arrays
topics.description: The most common interview surface. Prefix sums, difference arrays, in-place rearrangement, cyclic sort, Kadane's algorithm, and interval manipulation. Every problem here teaches you to exploit contiguous memory and index arithmetic.
learning_outcomes: Build prefix-sum and difference-array structures and recognize when they apply
Apply Kadane's algorithm and its 2D and circular variants
Rearrange arrays in-place using cyclic sort and Dutch National Flag
Merge, intersect, and reason about intervals

topics.name: Binary Search
topics.description: Halving the search space — on sorted arrays, on rotated arrays, on 2D matrices, and crucially on the *answer space* itself (parametric search). The skill being trained is identifying a monotonic predicate, not memorizing a template.
learning_outcomes: Implement bug-free `lower_bound` / `upper_bound` and stop confusing them
Search on rotated and bitonic arrays
Apply binary search on the answer space (e.g., minimum capacity, maximum value)
Use binary search inside larger algorithms (LIS, median of two arrays)

topics.name: Strings
topics.description: Strings are arrays with extra structure: character frequency, alphabets, prefixes/suffixes, palindromes. Covers frequency-counter techniques, palindrome expansion, KMP, Z-algorithm, and rolling hashes (Rabin–Karp).
learning_outcomes: Solve anagram and frequency-comparison problems with O(σ) extra space
Find palindromic substrings via expansion and Manacher's algorithm
Implement KMP failure function and Z-array, and use them for substring search
Apply rolling hashes for fast equality checks on substrings

topics.name: Linked List
topics.description: Pointer manipulation under constraint: no random access, only `next`. Trains you in dummy-node techniques, in-place reversal, fast/slow pointers, and rigorous null-handling. The patterns here transfer directly to graph traversal.
learning_outcomes: Reverse, split, and merge linked lists in O(1) extra space
Detect and locate cycles using Floyd's tortoise-and-hare
Use dummy/sentinel nodes to simplify edge cases
Manipulate doubly-linked lists for LRU-style structures

topics.name: Recursion
topics.description: Recursion as a first-class problem-solving tool: subset/permutation generation, decision-tree exploration, divide-and-conquer, and the foundation for backtracking, tree, and DP problems. Trains the mental discipline of trusting the recursion.
learning_outcomes: Write recursive solutions by trusting subproblem return contracts
Generate subsets, permutations, and combinations via choose/skip and swap-based recursion
Apply backtracking with proper state restoration
Distinguish divide-and-conquer from naive recursion via complexity analysis

topics.name: Bit Manipulation
topics.description: Working with bits: XOR identities, masks, single-number variants, counting set bits, bitmask DP, and subset enumeration via `sub = (sub - 1) & mask`. Teaches you to think of integers as 32-bit vectors.
learning_outcomes: Use XOR properties to find missing/duplicate elements without extra space
Manipulate individual bits with set/clear/toggle/test operations
Enumerate all submasks of a bitmask in O(3^N) total
Encode small-N state with bitmasks for DP

topics.name: Stack & Queue
topics.description: LIFO and FIFO structures, monotonic stacks, monotonic deques, parenthesis-style validation, expression evaluation, and the queue/stack trick (implementing one with the other). The monotonic-stack family alone solves a huge class of next-greater / histogram problems.
learning_outcomes: Recognize and apply the monotonic stack pattern (next-greater / next-smaller)
Use monotonic deques for sliding-window max/min in O(N)
Validate and evaluate bracketed and infix/postfix expressions
Implement stack-with-min, queue-from-stacks, and similar augmented structures

topics.name: Sliding Window & Two Pointers
topics.description: Two of the most powerful linear-time techniques. Sliding window converts O(N·K) and O(N²) brute-force scans into O(N) by maintaining a running aggregate over a moving range. Two pointers exploit sorted or monotonic structure to converge or scan in lockstep. Together they cover hundreds of interview problems.
learning_outcomes: Apply fixed-size sliding window to aggregate-over-range problems
Apply variable-size sliding window with shrink-on-violation
Use the at-most-K trick to count exactly-K subarrays in O(N)
Use converging and same-direction two pointers on sorted inputs
Recognize the structural signal that allows the linear-time technique

topics.name: Heaps
topics.description: Priority queues for top-K, k-way merge, scheduling, and the two-heap median trick. Also the supporting structure for Dijkstra and Prim. You learn to think of 'always pick the smallest/largest pending item' as a primitive.
learning_outcomes: Implement a binary heap by hand and reason about its O(log N) ops
Solve top-K problems with a size-K heap of opposite polarity
Merge K sorted streams in O(N log K)
Maintain a running median with two balanced heaps

topics.name: Greedy
topics.description: Local choices that provably give global optima. Covers the exchange-argument proof technique, interval scheduling, and the classic sort-then-pick patterns. The hard part is not implementation — it's *proving* the greedy choice is safe.
learning_outcomes: State and verify the greedy-choice property for a candidate algorithm
Solve interval scheduling, jump-game, and gas-station problems
Use sort-then-greedy with custom comparators
Distinguish problems that need DP from those where greedy is provably correct

topics.name: Binary Trees
topics.description: Recursive structures par excellence. DFS variants (pre/in/post-order), level-order BFS, height/diameter/path-sum recursion, ancestor problems, and serialization. Most tree problems are recursion problems with a particular state shape.
learning_outcomes: Implement all four traversal orders, both recursively and iteratively
Solve recursion-on-tree problems by defining a clean return contract
Find LCA, diameter, and root-to-leaf paths
Serialize and deserialize a binary tree

topics.name: BST
topics.description: Binary Search Trees: the in-order property, validation, ordered insertion/deletion, k-th smallest, and range queries. The skill is *exploiting* the BST invariant rather than treating the BST as a generic tree.
learning_outcomes: Validate a BST in a single traversal with bounded ranges
Insert and delete nodes while preserving the BST invariant
Find k-th smallest/largest via in-order with early termination
Solve range-sum and range-count problems on BSTs

topics.name: Graphs
topics.description: The most general structure. BFS shortest-path on unweighted graphs, DFS for connectivity and topo-sort, Union-Find for dynamic connectivity, Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford for weighted shortest paths, MST (Prim/Kruskal), bipartite checking, and SCC (Tarjan/Kosaraju). The capstone of classical algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Represent graphs with adjacency lists and matrices and choose between them
Run BFS, DFS, topological sort, and Union-Find on real problems
Implement Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford and know when each applies
Find MSTs and SCCs
Detect cycles in directed and undirected graphs

topics.name: Dynamic Programming
topics.description: Memoization and tabulation for problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Covers 1D / 2D / grid DP, knapsack variants, LIS, LCS, edit distance, partition DP, interval DP, bitmask DP, and tree DP. The largest topic; the most universally tested.
learning_outcomes: Define a DP state precisely and prove its correctness
Convert top-down memoization to bottom-up tabulation
Optimize space from O(N·M) to O(N) or O(1) via rolling arrays
Solve knapsack-family, sequence-alignment, partition, interval, bitmask, and tree DPs

topics.name: Tries
topics.description: Prefix trees for word/prefix lookup, autocomplete, word-search, and XOR-on-bits problems. A specialized but high-leverage structure: a single trie can replace dozens of hash-map operations.
learning_outcomes: Implement insert/search/startsWith on a character trie
Solve word-search-II by trie + DFS pruning
Use a binary trie of bit-strings to maximize XOR queries
Reason about trie space cost vs. hash-map alternatives
